title: Why did we multiply by three to change three fourths?
description: Three fourths is changed into nine twelfths by multiplying the top and the bottom by three. The board shows why three turns the bottom number four into a number that four and three both go into. Keeko's doubt is that only the bottom number needs to be multiplied.
teaching_notes: One idea: we multiply by the number that turns the bottom number into a common multiple, and we multiply the top by the same number to keep the fraction equal. Watch for students who multiply only the bottom number.

source: In 3/4 = (3×3)/(4×3) = 9/12, why did we choose to multiply both the numerator and denominator by 3?
video_script.why: The child sees why the multiplier is chosen: it turns the bottom number into a common multiple of both bottom numbers, and the top is multiplied by the same number so the fraction stays equal.
video_script.substitution: The book's own change of three fourths into nine twelfths, next to the other fraction two thirds.
video_script.anchor: a strip showing three fourths redrawn as nine twelfths, with two thirds waiting beside it
video_script.wrong_answer: multiply only the bottom by three
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies only the bottom number by three, so three fourths becomes three twelfths, a much smaller amount, and the fraction is no longer equal.
video_script.payoff_line: We multiplied by three to turn the bottom number four into twelve

final_answer.spoken: three, so that the bottom number four becomes twelve

video_script.fraction_reading: three fourths, nine twelfths, two thirds, three twelfths
hold_back: 12 is a common multiple of 4 and 3
never_show: the reason line before the answer beat
maths_rules: the other fraction is 2/3, with bottom number 3
4 × 3 = 12, and 12 is a common multiple of 4 and 3
multiplying the top and the bottom by 3 keeps the fraction equal
Keeko's slip: 3/12 is smaller than 3/4, because 12 parts are smaller than 4 parts
video_script.design: The strip for three fourths is cut into twelfths, and the multiplier three is shown on both the top and the bottom. The reason line stays hidden until the answer beat.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a strip showing 3/4 and below it the same strip cut into 12 parts showing 9/12; the words multiply the top and the bottom by 3

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.ask: the number 3 glows on the top and on the bottom

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about changing three fourths into nine twelfths.
<bookmark mark='change'/>We multiplied the top and the bottom by three.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Why did we choose three?

beats.on_screen: the strips hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: two words appear: equivalent fractions, equal in size; common multiple, a number that two numbers both go into; the number 6 for 2 and 3

marks.equal: the words equivalent fractions appear with two equal strips
marks.six: 6 appears with 2 going into it 3 times and 3 going into it 2 times

narration: <bookmark mark='equal'/>Fractions that are equal in size are called equivalent fractions.
<bookmark mark='multiple'/>A number that two numbers both go into is called a common multiple.
<bookmark mark='six'/>For example, six is a common multiple of two and three.

marks.given: the change of 3/4 into 9/12 and the other fraction 2/3 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three fourths was changed into nine twelfths, and we take away two thirds.

beats.on_screen: To find: why the multiplier is 3

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find why three was chosen.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: bottom numbers 4 and 3 are different

marks.two: the bottom numbers 4 and 3 glow in turn

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step one, notice that the bottom numbers four and three are different.
Pieces of different sizes cannot be taken away, so both fractions need one new bottom number.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: a number that 4 and 3 both go into: (4 × 3) gives 12

marks.find: the question a number that 4 and 3 both go into appears
marks.twelve: the product of 4 and 3 is written as 12 and glows

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>Step two, look for a number that both four and three go into.
<bookmark mark='twelve'/>Four times three is twelve, and four and three both go into twelve.

marks.bottom: the bottom 4 is multiplied by 3 and becomes 12
marks.top: the top 3 is multiplied by 3 and becomes 9

narration: <bookmark mark='bottom'/>Step three, turn the bottom number four into twelve by multiplying by three.
<bookmark mark='top'/>Multiply the top by three too, to keep the fraction equal. Three times three is nine.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so 9/12 is 3/4 again
narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step four, check the new fraction is equal. Divide nine and twelve by three.
<bookmark mark='again'/>Nine divided by three is three, and twelve divided by three is four. We get three fourths again.

beats.on_screen: Answer: multiply by 3 because 4 × 3 = 12, and 12 is a common multiple of 4 and 3

marks.ans: the reason line is written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>We multiplied by three to turn the bottom number four into twelve.
<bookmark mark='unit'/>Twelve is a common multiple of four and three, so both fractions can use the unit one twelfth.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the strips
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 3/4 becomes 3/12; a strip of 3 thin twelfths sits beside the strip of 3 fourths and is much shorter; the bubble is struck through

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows only the bottom multiplied by 3, giving 3/12
marks.small: 3 thin twelfths appear next to 3 fourths and look much shorter
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and the top is multiplied by 3 as well

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we multiply only the bottom by three.
Then three fourths becomes three twelfths.
<bookmark mark='small'/>But three twelfths is three thin pieces, much less than three fourths.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Changing only the bottom changes the amount. The top must be multiplied by three too.
